title: Metal Stud Framing
short_answer: Layout the whole floor first, then build by operation — all bottoms, all tops, all studs — not wall-by-wall.
summary: Lay out the whole floor first. Then build by operation, not by wall.
plain_words: You mark every wall on the floor first, for the whole floor. Then you go around and set all the bottom track. Then all the top track. Then fill in all the studs. One tool in your hand at a time, one motion repeated. It feels slower and it isn't — the walking and the tool-swapping is what costs the money, not the screwing.
when_to_use: Starting metal stud framing on a floor or area
Before hanging — framing must be true with backing in
Job Check Framing Status is the gate for hang
prerequisites: Current drawing set and wall-type legend
Door/frame schedule and backing list from casework drawings

tools.name: Chop saw / snips for track and stud
Camera for backing + rated photo record

materials.name: Track and stud per wall type (gauge/width)
Deflection track / head-of-wall materials per detail

steps.body: Pull the current drawing set and confirm the revision.
Find the building control lines / column grid. Every dimension comes off grid — never off an existing wall or a slab edge. Existing walls lie.
Verify control is square: 3-4-5 at the biggest multiple that fits — 12-16-20
Shoot the slab along the wall runs for high spots and dips.
Read the wall type legend: gauge, width, spacing, height (to ceiling vs. to deck), rating.
Confirm the head-of-wall detail. This one detail governs your whole top track operation.
Get the door/frame schedule for rough opening dimensions.
Build the backing list from casework and equipment drawings — before layout.
Snap the primary control line off grid, then a perpendicular. Verify square before snapping anything else.
Chain every wall from a single reference point. Never measure wall-to-wall cumulatively — error stacks down the corridor.
Snap both faces, or one line plus a keel X on the track side. Pick one convention for the whole crew.
Write the wall type on the slab: A1 · 3-5/8 25GA @16 · 1HR · TO DECK
Mark every opening with its rough opening dimension and swing.
Mark off-module studs now: jambs, corners, intersections, backing.
Transfer to the deck with a plumb laser as you go. Coming back later means a second lift trip for every wall.
Walk the layout with the super before any track goes down.
Count studs off the layout on the floor, not the plan. You just walked it.
Drop bundles at the walls they belong to. Cut a story pole for the repeat stud length.
Track tight to the line, all of it, before you look at a top track.
Run long and continuous; lap splices per spec, don't butt them.
Fastener spacing per the approved submittal, plus one near every end and splice.
Rated walls: track sits in the sealant bed per the listed detail. Not retrofittable.
Build the head of wall per the approved detail, not per habit. See the systems reference below.
Studs cut short of the track web by the gap the detail calls for.
Rated walls: the head-of-wall joint is a listed assembly. Build it as listed.
Photograph the head of wall as you go, by area.
Pass one: stand loose studs in the track down every wall, roughly spaced. No measuring, no screws.
Pass two: set exact spacing and fasten.
Every stud open side the same direction, facing the run. MEP and board hangers both depend on it.
Line the knockouts up down the wall so the electrician pulls straight.
Attachment per the submittal — see the note below, it's a large labor number.
At deflection heads, fasten only where the detail permits so the joint can move.
RO = frame dimension plus the manufacturer's clearance. Off the schedule, never guessed.
Jamb studs per the detail — doubled, boxed, or heavier gauge. Wider and heavier doors take more.
Header track over the opening, cripples above back on module.
Check every opening plumb and square as you build it, not at punch.

Work from the written list, not memory: casework, countertops, grab bars, handrails, TVs and mounts, wall-hung fixtures, headwalls, marker boards, signage, corner guards, door stops, extinguisher cabinets.
Heights from the casework/equipment shop drawings when they exist — they beat the elevations.
Keel-mark every backing location on the stud face.
Photograph every wall with backing, tagged by room, before it's covered.
String line or laser the walls — straight and plumb.
Every RO: dimension, plumb, square, header, jambs.
All backing in, right height, marked.
No stud hard-bearing on a deflection track anywhere.
Bridging/bracing installed and anchored per the detail.
Photo record, then framing inspection — before rock.

warnings.title: Hard-bearing on deflection track
warnings.body: Studs must not hard-bear on a deflection / slip track. That kills the joint’s movement and fails inspection.

warnings.title: Layout off a crooked wall
warnings.body: Every dimension comes off grid — never off an existing wall or a slab edge that isn’t control.

warnings.title: Wall-by-wall tool swapping
warnings.body: Batch by operation. Walking and tool-swapping costs more than fastening.

variations.title: Tall / stacked walls
variations.when: Walls above stock stud length or multi-story stacked
changes: Confirm L/240 vs L/360 before arguing with the GC

variations.title: Rated / shaft walls
changes: Assembly tag governs gauge, spacing, liner, HOWall

quality_checks.prompt: Plumb and straight; no twisted studs
Backing installed and photographed before board
No stud hard-bearing on deflection track

common_mistakes.title: Framing off the slab edge
common_mistakes.wrong: Snap from a crooked existing wall

common_mistakes.title: Missing backing
common_mistakes.wrong: Hang then discover no grab-bar backing
common_mistakes.right: Backing list before layout; photo before close

troubleshooting.symptom: Track won’t sit flat on slab
troubleshooting.fix: Shoot slab along runs; grind or shim per detail — don’t force twisted track
